title: Firewalls, IDS & IPS
summary: The network's gatekeeper and the alarms that ring for intruders.

pages.title: Firewall: the traffic guard
pages.body:
A firewall inspects incoming and outgoing traffic and decides to allow or block it based on rules: IP address, port, protocol, or application.

Healthy rules usually:
- Deny all inbound by default
- Open only the ports actually used, e.g. 443 for web
- Restrict admin access (SSH, remote desktop) to specific addresses

Home routers and Windows have built-in firewalls too. Keep them on.
pages.tip: A firewall is the neighborhood gate guard with a guest list. Not on the list, not getting in.

pages.title: Next-gen firewalls & WAFs
pages.body:
Classic firewalls only look at addresses and ports. Modern (next-gen) firewalls recognize applications and traffic content.

A WAF (Web Application Firewall) specifically protects web apps. It can block requests that look like SQL injection or XSS before they reach the app.

But a WAF doesn't replace secure code. Treat it as an extra layer.
pages.tip: A regular guard checks ID cards. A sharp guard also checks bags.

pages.title: IDS and IPS
pages.body:
- IDS (Intrusion Detection System): monitors and raises alerts on attack patterns, but doesn't block
- IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): like an IDS, but blocks suspicious traffic immediately

Both recognize attacks via:
- Signatures: known attack patterns
- Anomalies: behavior that deviates from normal

The challenge: too many false positives make teams careless.
pages.tip: An IDS is a burglar alarm. An IPS is an alarm that also locks the doors automatically.

quiz.prompt: A healthy firewall rule for inbound traffic is...
quiz.explanation: Default deny minimizes open doors.

quiz.prompt: A WAF specifically protects...
quiz.explanation: A WAF filters malicious requests to web apps.

quiz.prompt: The difference between IDS and IPS?
options: IDS alerts; IPS also blocks immediately
quiz.explanation: Prevention means actively stopping it.

quiz.prompt: Signature-based detection recognizes...
quiz.explanation: Brand-new attacks need anomaly detection.

quiz.prompt: Why are too many false positives dangerous?
options: Teams get careless and miss real alerts
quiz.explanation: When alarms ring constantly, people stop paying attention.

title: VPN & Zero Trust
summary: Encrypted tunnels, and why "inside the network" doesn't mean safe.

pages.title: VPN: an encrypted tunnel
pages.body:
A VPN wraps all your traffic in an encrypted tunnel to a VPN server, which then forwards it to the internet.

Benefits:
- People on the same Wi-Fi can't snoop
- Employees can reach the office network safely from home

What to understand: the VPN provider can now see your traffic. So choose a trusted one, not a free VPN with an unknown owner.
pages.tip: A VPN is a covered toll road. Bystanders can't see your car, but the toll operator knows you passed.

pages.title: VPN myths
pages.body:
A VPN isn't an invisibility cloak:
- It doesn't make you fully anonymous; logging into accounts still identifies you
- It doesn't protect against phishing or malware
- It doesn't make fake sites safe

VPNs are most useful on public Wi-Fi, for reaching office networks, and for hiding activity from the local network.
pages.tip: A raincoat keeps you dry, but it doesn't make you immune to traffic accidents.

pages.title: Zero Trust
pages.body:
The old model: "inside the office network = trusted". The problem: once an attacker gets in, they roam freely.

Zero Trust flips that: never trust automatically, always verify.
- Every access checks identity (usually with MFA)
- The device is checked for health
- Access rights are minimal
- Activity is continuously monitored

Many companies are moving from office VPNs to this model.
pages.tip: Zero Trust is a building where every door needs a card tap, not just the front door.

quiz.prompt: A VPN works by...
options: Wrapping traffic in an encrypted tunnel
quiz.explanation: Traffic is encrypted up to the VPN server.

quiz.prompt: Who can see your traffic when using a VPN?
quiz.explanation: Trust shifts to the VPN provider.

quiz.prompt: Does a VPN protect against phishing?
options: No; fake sites can still fool you
quiz.explanation: A VPN protects the path, not your decision to enter data.

quiz.prompt: Zero Trust's core principle is...
quiz.explanation: Network location doesn't grant trust by itself.

quiz.prompt: The weakness of the old "inside = safe" model is...
options: An attacker inside can move freely
quiz.explanation: This is called lateral movement.

title: Device Hardening
summary: Tightening your phone and laptop so they're hard to break into.

pages.title: What hardening is
pages.body:
Hardening means shrinking the attack surface by switching off what's unnecessary and strengthening what's used.

Principles:
- Unused: remove or disable it
- Used: update it and configure it securely
- Access: grant as little as possible

The fewer doors, the fewer there are to guard.
pages.tip: A house with two doors is easier to guard than one with ten open windows.

pages.title: Android phone checklist
pages.body:
- Automatic system and app updates
- Screen lock with a 6+ digit PIN or biometrics, short screen timeout
- Remove unused apps
- Review permissions: location, microphone, camera, SMS, Accessibility
- Play Protect on, "unknown apps" off
- Private DNS (e.g. dns.adguard.com or one.one.one.one) for extra filtering
- Turn off Bluetooth and NFC when unused
- Enable Find My Device
pages.tip: Like tidying a room: toss what you don't use, lock the valuable drawers.

pages.title: Laptop checklist
pages.body:
- Update the OS and browser
- Daily account without admin rights
- Built-in firewall and antivirus (Windows Defender) on
- Disk encryption: BitLocker (Windows) or FileVault (Mac)
- Auto screen lock when you step away (Windows + L)
- Remove unused software and browser extensions
- Avoid pirated software; it's one of the biggest malware sources
- Regular backups to a drive you unplug afterwards
pages.tip: An encrypted, locked laptop is like a stolen safe: heavy, but the contents stay protected.

quiz.prompt: Hardening means...
options: Shrinking the attack surface and tightening settings
quiz.explanation: A smaller attack surface is harder to attack.

quiz.prompt: Why remove apps you don't use?
quiz.explanation: Abandoned apps can carry flaws and excess permissions.

quiz.prompt: Windows' built-in disk encryption is...
quiz.explanation: BitLocker encrypts the whole disk.

quiz.prompt: The quick shortcut to lock a Windows screen?
quiz.explanation: Make it a habit whenever you step away.

quiz.prompt: Why shouldn't your daily account be an admin?
options: Malware running under it is limited too
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits damage.

title: Passkeys & Password Managers
summary: The future of logging in without stealable passwords.

pages.title: Password managers
pages.body:
Nobody can remember dozens of long, unique passwords. A password manager stores them in an encrypted vault opened with one master password (plus 2FA).

Benefits:
- Generates long random passwords automatically
- Autofills only on the correct domain, which helps reject phishing sites
- Alerts you if a password has leaked

Examples: Bitwarden, Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain.
pages.tip: A password manager is one safe for all your keys. You only need to guard the safe's key very well.

pages.title: Passkeys: logging in with public keys
pages.body:
Passkeys replace passwords with a cryptographic key pair:
- The private key stays safely on your phone or laptop, never sent
- The server stores only the public key
- Logging in = your phone signs a challenge from the server, unlocked with fingerprint or PIN

Since no secret is typed or sent, passkeys can't be phished and are useless to attackers if the server's database leaks.
pages.tip: A passkey is like a personal stamp. The server only keeps a sample impression to compare; the stamp stays in your hand.

pages.title: Getting started
pages.body:
Practical steps:
- Turn on passkeys for accounts that support them: Google, Apple, Microsoft, GitHub, and more every month
- Use a password manager for accounts without passkey support
- Secure your main account (email) first, since it's the key to resetting every other account
- Store recovery codes somewhere safe and offline

Priority order: email, Google/Apple account, banks & e-wallets, social media.
pages.tip: The most important key is the one that can copy all your other keys: your email.

quiz.prompt: Why does a password manager help against phishing?
options: It only autofills on the correct domain
quiz.explanation: If autofill doesn't appear, the domain is different.

quiz.prompt: With passkeys, the server stores...
quiz.explanation: The private key never leaves your device.

quiz.prompt: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
options: No secret is typed or sent to the site
quiz.explanation: A fake site can't fish for something you never type.

quiz.prompt: The first account to secure is...
quiz.explanation: Email is used to reset other accounts' passwords.

quiz.prompt: Recovery codes should be kept...
quiz.explanation: Backup codes can open the account without 2FA.

title: Defense in Depth & Awareness
summary: No single tool is perfect, so stack them. And people are the key layer.

pages.title: Defense in depth
pages.body:
Every safeguard has gaps. Defense in depth stacks many layers so if one fails, others still hold:
- People: training and safe habits
- Devices: updates, antivirus, encryption
- Apps: secure code, WAF
- Network: firewalls, segmentation
- Data: encryption, backups, access rights

An attacker has to get through every layer, not just one.
pages.tip: Like slices of Swiss cheese: each has holes, but stacked up, the holes rarely line up.

pages.title: People: the strongest or weakest layer
pages.body:
Most incidents involve a human factor: clicking phishing links, weak passwords, misconfigurations, or falling for fake calls.

But trained people are also the best detectors. An employee who gets suspicious and reports it can stop an attack faster than any tool.

A healthy culture: report without fear of punishment. People afraid of being scolded tend to hide mistakes.
pages.tip: The best guard still loses to an employee who holds the door for an unknown "courier".

pages.title: Small habits, big impact
pages.body:
The five habits that save the most people:
- Pause 10 seconds before clicking, transferring, or sharing a code
- Verify through another channel (call the official number, meet in person)
- One account, one password, using a password manager
- 2FA or passkeys on important accounts
- Regular updates and backups

Security isn't about paranoia; it's about habits.
pages.tip: Wearing a helmet doesn't make you afraid of riding. It lets you ride with peace of mind.

quiz.prompt: Defense in depth means...
quiz.explanation: If one layer fails, others still protect.

quiz.prompt: Why does a "report without fear" culture matter?
options: People report sooner, so attacks stop sooner
quiz.explanation: Fear makes people hide mistakes.

quiz.prompt: The simplest habit before transferring due to an urgent message?
options: Pause and verify through another channel
quiz.explanation: Urgency is a scammer's main weapon.

quiz.prompt: The Swiss cheese analogy describes...
options: Stacked holey layers rarely having aligned holes
quiz.explanation: A well-known model for explaining layered defense.

quiz.prompt: The "data" layer is protected with...
quiz.explanation: Data is what attackers ultimately want.

title: Windows & Active Directory
summary: Accounts, event logs, and the brain of office networks.

pages.title: Accounts and rights on Windows
pages.body:
Windows has two main account types:
- Standard: for daily work, can't change system settings
- Administrator: can install software and change anything

UAC (the "Do you want to allow this app..." window) appears when something needs admin rights. It isn't a nuisance; it's an emergency brake. If it pops up when you aren't installing anything, be suspicious.

Check accounts on a computer from Command Prompt:
$ net user
$ whoami /groups
pages.tip: UAC is a guard asking "really open the safe?". Don't say yes if you aren't doing anything.

pages.title: Event Viewer: Windows' CCTV
pages.body:
Windows records important activity in Event Viewer (type eventvwr in Start). Windows Logs → Security holds login records.

Event IDs worth knowing:
- 4624: successful logon
- 4625: failed logon
- 4720: a user account was created
- 4732: an account was added to a group (e.g. Administrators)

Many 4625s in a row then a 4624 = a password guess that worked, just like in LV.04. A new account you didn't create = a red flag.
pages.tip: Event Viewer is a digital guest book. A name you don't recognize means an uninvited guest.

pages.title: Active Directory: the office network's brain
pages.body:
In offices, hundreds of computers and accounts are managed centrally through Active Directory (AD):
- Domain Controller: the server that stores every account and checks logins
- Users & Groups: employee accounts grouped, e.g. "Finance" or "IT"
- Group Policy (GPO): rules enforced on every computer, e.g. a minimum password length

Since AD holds every key, it's attackers' prime target. Common attacks: password spraying (one common password tried against many accounts) and stealing domain admin accounts.

Defenses: MFA, strong passwords, admin accounts separate from daily ones, and least privilege.
pages.tip: AD is HR and the building's key room combined. Whoever controls that room controls the whole building.

quiz.prompt: A UAC prompt appears when you aren't installing anything. You should...
quiz.explanation: A sudden admin request may come from malware.

quiz.prompt: Event ID 4625 in the Windows Security log means...
quiz.explanation: 4624 is success, 4625 is failure.

quiz.prompt: The server that stores accounts and checks logins in Active Directory is the...
quiz.explanation: The Domain Controller is AD's authentication hub.

quiz.prompt: Password spraying means...
options: Trying many passwords on one account
Trying one common password on many accounts
quiz.explanation: It avoids lockouts since each account is tried only once.

quiz.prompt: Why keep admin accounts separate from daily accounts?
options: So a breached daily account doesn't carry admin rights
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits damage.
